newsitem.title: UK: Ex-UK to Asia/Mideast air rates hit by excess capacity.
newsitem.headline: Ex-UK to Asia/Mideast air rates hit by excess capacity.

text.p: Increased capacity on routes from the UK to Asia and the Middle East along with the continued strength of sterling has forced air cargo rates lower, a Reuters survey showed.
Seasonally May is a quiet month and some carriers said they expect the slack in the market to last until mid-June after which they hope to see a pick-up in rates.
The rate cutting has focused on shipments of 500 kilos or more. Rates for freight carried in passenger bellyholds has not been subject to the same pressure, carriers said.

Continued special promotional offers from British Airways remain a factor. These offered low rates for pallets and consolidators have allowed these to trickle down to lower weights although the greatest reductions are for pallet or bins - the most common is pallet class 5 which typically has a maximum gross weight of five to six tonnes.

Amongst some very low rates talked of ex-UK were 90 pence a kilo to Melbourne and 36 pence to Cairo but industry sources said these were exceptional. Typically shipments of 500 to 1,000 kgs could find rates as much as 20 pence below rates for 100 kg shipments on Asian routes - although hard to generalise, carriers said a normal differential is closer to ten pence.
On several Middle East routes carriers admitted having surplus capacity and, depending on the airline, were discounting or just holding rates on their home route.

Rates to the Indian sub-continent were also under pressure and again carriers and forwarders said this was most transparent for larger shipments where carriers competed most when seeking to fill freighters.

Additionally capacity has come in recent months from Polar Air Cargo to Korea and Japan, Air China to Hong Kong whilst Air Hong Kong is adding an ex-UK to Hong Kong. Asiana adds a weekly combi from Frankfurt later this month adding to the overall ex-Europe capacity to Asia, carriers said.

UAE state carrier Emirates is also adding capacity to Dubai by increasing its airbus flights from Manchester to a daily flight from the current five a week. Some of the bellyhold cargo capacity is being shared with Zurich, an Emirates official said.

Other extra capacity may come from Lufthansa flying into Ireland's Shannon airport. Industry talk has it that Singapore Airlines may up its Irish service which includes Amsterdam and Dubai to three times a week from two at present with some suggesting a tie-up with Aer Lingus.

In contrast Cathay Pacific has already responded to the surplus capacity to Asia and next month drops a 747-200F to Hong Kong ex-Heathrow, leaving four such flights a week equating to a tonnage reduction of 50-60 tonnes a week. This flight is being switched to Chicago.
Korean Air Lines UK cargo sales manager Frank Smith said he is chasing the opportunity of three charters of horses to Korea from Ireland likely during the course of this year.
Smith said dedicated charters of 747-200 freighters would be able to carry 29 pallets each capable of taking three horses.
Strength of sterling was having an impact on Korean import demand as has recent government moves to slow the Korean economy.
UK rates to Korea are being pressured by spot pricing by several airlines and this is forcing rates lower.
Some carriers said that in comparison the Japanese market was holding up well although several instances of carriers cutting rates to fill planes were quoted.

Air New Zealand's Phil Rawlings who is cargo sales manager for Europe said it has found found continuing demand for its capacity to New Zealand fdrom the UK but added that this long-haul flight via Los Angeles is finding business much more erratic to the U.S. west coast.
Virgin Atlantic Airways last week said it is considering starting regular freighter flights between the UK and an unnamed Far Eastern destination later this year with wet-leased aircraft.
"A freighter proposal is currently on the table and its viability is being evaluated," said cargo general manager marketing David Woodward.

If the go-ahead were given, a Boeing 747F or MD-11 freighter would be used, wet-leased from a specialist operator. Wet-leasing covers the hire of both aircraft and crew and usually also includes insurance and maintenance.
"It must revolve around commercial demand...the be all and end all is commercial viability. I believe the demand is there (for a freighter operation), as is the revenue to sustain it," he added.

Woodward declined to name the proposed destination but said that Virgin's current Asian routes -- from London Heathrow to Tokyo and Hong Kong -- were attracting good bellyhold cargo traffic and yields, particularly to and from Japan.
He added that Virgin's UK-Japan cargo yields were up 4.3 percent in the first four months of this year compared to the same period in 1996, but declined to give details.
Virgin's Woodward said that London-Hong Kong was "still a good cargo market" for the airline.
"But unfortunately, we are hampered by inconsistent uplift in both directions," caused by restricted aircraft performance on a long, diverse routing, he said.
He added he expected that air cargo demand in Hong Kong would continue as normal after the British colony is handed over to China at midnight on Monday, June 30.
"We believe that for quite a while, the market will remain pretty similar to what it is now," said Woodward.
"A lot of air cargo business that passes through Hong Kong originates in China. We believe that in the longer term, there will be a shift of this business to mainland China airports," he said.
Woodward said this depended very much on improvements in customs delays in China which he said continued to be a major problem confronting airlines and forwarders serving that market.

"It can take up to 15 days to clear airfreight goods into and out of China," he said. "Once this situation is improved, I am sure we will see a drift in cargo from Hong Kong to mainland China airports."
